name: Coverage and Mutation Testing
intent: Read code coverage as a map of what the tests never run, not a measure of what they check, and use mutation testing to ask whether the tests would notice if the code were wrong.
scenario: A 12-line discount function is tested by four suites: one that calls it and asserts nothing, one with a single assertion per path, one with edge cases, and one that checks 60 generated inputs against a reference. All four reach 100% line coverage. The team then changes the code in 10 small ways and counts how many changes each suite notices.
problem: Line coverage is defined as the share of lines that ran during the tests, and a high number is often read as a high-quality suite. The trap is in the word ran. A test that calls a function and never asserts anything executes every line and checks none of them. Coverage can only tell you that a line was not run, which is useful, never that it was verified. Mutation testing asks the question coverage cannot: if this line were wrong, would any test fail? It makes small changes to the code, such as flipping a comparison or deleting a constant, and counts how many of those mutants the tests kill. In its simplest form it costs a full test run per mutant, and some mutants cannot be killed because they change nothing observable.

howItWorks.title: Measure what ran
howItWorks.text: A coverage tool records which lines, or branches, execute while the tests run. The report shows the gaps: code no test reaches. A gap is a real signal, since nothing checks that code at all. A line that is covered tells you only that it ran.

howItWorks.title: See how a covered line can be unchecked
howItWorks.text: A test that calls the function and ignores the result, or that asserts something loose such as a non-null value, covers every line it passes through and verifies nothing. Padding a suite with such tests raises the coverage number and leaves the risk where it was.

howItWorks.title: Change the code and see if the tests notice
howItWorks.text: Mutation testing makes one small change at a time: turn a >= into a >, a + into a -, a 10 into a 0, a condition into its negation. Each changed copy is a mutant. A mutant is killed when at least one test fails on it, and survives when every test still passes. The share of mutants killed is the mutation score.

howItWorks.title: Read the survivors
howItWorks.text: A surviving mutant points at a behaviour that no test pins down: a boundary, a constant, a rounding rule. Write the test that kills it, and the suite gets better in a specific way. Some survivors are equivalent mutants that change the code but not its observable behaviour, and no test can kill them, so a score of exactly 100% is often out of reach.

howItWorks.title: Pay for it where it matters
howItWorks.text: In its simplest form, mutation testing runs the whole suite once for every mutant, so the cost is the number of tests times the number of mutants plus one. Real tools cut this by running only the tests that reach the changed line and stopping at the first failure, but the cost still grows with the number of mutants. Teams limit it to the code that matters most, to the files changed in a pull request, or to a smaller set of mutation operators, and accept a narrower view for a cheaper run. Some teams skip it and rely on review and coverage gaps, which trades certainty for time.

pros: Coverage gaps point at code that no test can possibly protect
Mutation score measures whether tests would detect a defect, which coverage cannot
Each surviving mutant names a concrete missing test, such as an unpinned boundary
Running it on changed code in a pull request is a practical way to review test quality
cons: Coverage is easy to inflate with tests that assert nothing, especially when it is a target
Mutation testing is slow: up to one full test run per mutant
Equivalent mutants cannot be killed, so a score needs interpretation
A high mutation score still checks only the changes the tool tried, not every possible defect
whenToUse: Reviewing a critical piece of logic, such as pricing, permissions or parsing, where a quiet mistake is costly
Looking for code with no tests at all, using a coverage report
A team has a coverage target and wants to know whether the tests behind it are meaningful
whenNotToUse: As a target to maximise on its own: a number that becomes a target tends to get gamed
Mutation testing on a slow end-to-end suite where each mutant costs minutes
Code with no stable behaviour to pin down, such as generated code or thin glue
pitfalls: 100% line coverage from tests that call the code and assert nothing: in the model, the mutation score of such a suite is 0%
Setting a coverage target and then padding the suite with assertion-free tests to meet it
Reading an uncovered line as a bug and a covered line as safe, when covered means only that it ran
Chasing a mutation score of 100% and spending hours on equivalent mutants that cannot be killed
Writing the expected values by copying the code's output, so the test agrees with whatever the code does
Running full mutation testing on every commit of a large codebase and finding the pipeline too slow to keep

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Writes the code and the tests.

roles.label: Test suite
roles.description: The tests whose strength is being measured.

roles.label: Mutation tool
roles.description: Makes one small change at a time and reruns the tests.

quiz.question: A suite calls the discount function with three inputs and asserts nothing. The coverage report says 100%. What does that tell you?
options: Every line ran, but nothing was checked, so a change that only alters the result would still pass.
The discount logic is fully verified, since all lines were reached.
The suite is slow, because it reaches every line.
The suite would catch a wrong boundary but not a wrong constant.
quiz.explanation: Coverage counts lines that ran, not lines that were checked. Without assertions, a change that only alters the returned value cannot make a test fail; only a crash or a hang could. A mutation run shows this as 0 of 10 mutants killed.

quiz.question: After a mutation run, one mutant survives: a >= was changed to > and every test passed. What is the most useful reading?
options: The tool is faulty and the mutant should be ignored.
No test pins down the boundary value, so add one with the input exactly at the boundary.
The code is correct, because the tests still pass.
The suite needs more tests that do not check boundaries.
quiz.explanation: A surviving mutant shows a behaviour that is not pinned. A test with the exact boundary input kills it. Not every survivor is real: an equivalent mutant changes nothing observable, which you can check by reasoning about it.

quiz.question: Why is a mutation run so much more expensive than a normal test run?
options: It compiles the code with debug symbols, which is slow.
It records a line for every statement, which adds overhead.
It needs a different test framework.
It runs the tests again for every mutant, so the cost grows with tests times mutants.
quiz.explanation: Each mutant needs the tests run against it. In the model, 60 tests and 10 mutants cost 60 x 11 = 660 test runs, against 60 for a normal run. That is why teams narrow it to changed code or fewer operators.
